analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals, labs, imaging centers, surgery centers, and insurers to post real prices online and fines those that don't.
analysis.headline: The Senate Health Committee approved this bipartisan price-transparency bill on July 22, 2026 and it now sits on the Senate calendar waiting for a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill forces hospitals, clinical labs, imaging providers, and surgery centers to publish all their prices — list prices, discounted cash prices, and the rates they negotiated with each insurer — in plain and machine-readable formats. Hospitals must actually honor the discounted cash price they post. Insurers must offer a real-time tool showing what a plan member would pay for a given service, and must publish their negotiated rates and drug payments in downloadable files. It also voids contract clauses that stop employers and health plans from seeing claims data and fees charged by pharmacy benefit managers and claims processors, and sets fines for those that refuse.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, especially the uninsured and people paying cash, who would finally see and be charged the posted cash price for care. People with insurance would get real-time estimates of what a plan covers and owes, including whether prior authorization applies. Employers that self-insure their workers would gain the right to audit claims data and fees held by pharmacy benefit managers and third-party administrators.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals must publish, monthly and free of charge, gross charges, discounted cash prices, and payer-specific negotiated rates for every item and service, in both a machine-readable spreadsheet and a consumer-friendly format, and a CEO must attest the data is accurate on pain of the attestation being 'material' to federal payment.
A hospital must accept its posted discounted cash price as payment in full from any patient who pays cash, regardless of insurance coverage.

Hospitals face penalties scaled to size — up to $35 per bed per day, and $5–10 million for large hospitals that are knowingly and willfully noncompliant twice in a year — with annual compliance reviews and no authority for the Secretary to waive the penalties.
Clinical diagnostic labs, imaging providers, and surgery centers connected to a hospital must post the same price information, with fines up to $300 per day for noncompliance.

Health plans must provide a real-time self-service tool showing the in-network rate, the member's cost sharing, accumulated deductible progress, and any prior-authorization or step-therapy requirements — and must hold the member harmless if the tool understates what is later billed.

Health plans must submit monthly machine-readable files disclosing negotiated in-network rates by provider, drugs' net prices after rebates and discounts, and out-of-network allowed amounts, with government audits of at least 20 plans per year and penalties up to $300 per member per day or $10 million.

Contracts may no longer gag employer plans: pharmacy benefit managers, third-party administrators, and provider networks must hand over claims data, payment formulas, and fee schedules, with gag clauses void as against public policy and a $10,000-per-day penalty for violations.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, third-party administrators, labs, and imaging providers, who must restructure contracts and data systems to disclose prices and face escalating fines for noncompliance. Hospitals would lose the ability to charge cash patients more than the posted discounted price.

drawbacks.text: Posting prices does not by itself lower them: past hospital price-transparency rules have seen weak compliance and little patient use, and the bill's heaviest penalty still tops out at $35 per bed per day for a large hospital — a modest sum for a big health system's revenues, which is why the law doubles down on audits and attestations instead of relying on consumer shopping.

Publishing every negotiated rate and contract formula could weaken insurers' bargaining position — hospitals can see what competitors settled for — and it imposes real compliance costs on providers and plans, costs that could be passed into premiums.

The out-of-network payment files break down amounts paid by each provider identified by national provider identifier, which could raise privacy and sensitivity concerns even though the plan-level files are the ones audited.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, documented problem: patients cannot learn what care costs, and cash-pay patients can be charged far more than insurers pay for the same service. The design is stronger than the existing transparency rules — it requires enforcement audits, personal executive attestations, and non-waivable penalties rather than just posting rules. The main honest objection is that price disclosure alone rarely forces prices down; the bill's leverage is mostly through embarrassment, employers auditing their own plans, and modest fines. Even on that view, the cost side falls on large, concentrated providers and payers rather than on patients.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Health Committee approved it with a bipartisan vote in July 2026 and placed it on the Senate's calendar, where it waits for the chamber's leaders to schedule a floor vote that hasn't happened yet.

narrative.text: Senator Roger Marshall introduced the bill on July 17, 2025 with cosponsors from both parties, including Democrats such as Booker, Warren, and Fetterman and Republicans such as Grassley and Ernst.
It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which held hearings on March 19, 2026.

On July 22, 2026 the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and on July 27, 2026 Senator Cassidy reported it — notably without a written committee report — and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar as Calendar No. 522.
No floor vote has occurred; the Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill is still alive.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, hospitals, insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers are better off: they continue operating under the current, weakly enforced transparency rules while the stronger version waits on the calendar. Transparency advocates did win full committee approval with a bipartisan coalition.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor is a Republican and the cosponsor list splits 13 Democrats to 11 Republicans; the bill cleared the HELP committee with a Republican chair reporting it, so no party bloc opposed it on the record.

industries.note: The bill requires hospitals to publish every charge, cash price, and insurer-negotiated rate, honor the cash price as payment in full, pass annual compliance reviews with CEO attestations, and pay fines up to $35 per bed per day or $5–10 million for repeat willful noncompliance. Patients paying cash are the direct beneficiaries, since they currently face opaque chargemaster prices.

Plans must run a real-time cost-sharing tool that holds members harmless for underestimates, publish monthly machine-readable files of negotiated rates and drug net prices, and face audits and fines up to $300 per member per day or $10 million. Their pricing currently relies on the confidentiality of these same rates.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and third-party administrators
industries.note: Gag clauses that keep employer plans from seeing claims data, fee schedules, and rebate flows are voided, with a $10,000-per-day penalty, quarterly disclosure of all rebates and remuneration, and the right of plans to choose their own auditors. These firms have profited from limited employer visibility into their fees.
Standalone labs and imaging providers must post prices for scheduled tests and imaging services and accept the posted cash price, with $300-per-day fines for noncompliance.

Employers that fund their own health plans gain enforceable rights to claims data, payment formulas, and fee disclosures from PBMs and administrators, which they can use to audit and renegotiate what they pay for employee care.

analysis.trajectory: Bipartisan committee approvals do not guarantee floor time in the Senate, and Calendar No. 522 does not itself schedule a vote. The bill's realistic paths are a unanimous-consent agreement, attachment to a larger year-end health or spending package, or dying on the calendar at the end of the 119th Congress in January 2027 — the most common fate for committee-reported bills that lack dedicated floor time.
